lines.text: Hi, I'm Sindy! Let's put sind into your CI pipeline.
Your code submits Slurm jobs, so every CI run should test it against a real cluster. How do you get one on a plain runner?
On GitHub, the sind action does both steps for you: install sind, and create your clusters in the workflow.
Standard Ubuntu runners on x sixty-four or ARM do the job: no sudo, no privileged containers, no custom images.
Elsewhere, any CI with a rootful Docker daemon will do. Download the release binary, and verify its provenance with the GitHub CLI.
Then sind doctor checks the prerequisites, and sind create cluster builds the cluster from your config.
Jobs that share a Docker daemon, as on a self-hosted runner, should each use their own realm, with the sind realm variable.
Within one realm, the lock stops jobs from breaking each other's mesh, but a delete cluster all in one job would remove the others' clusters too.
Every node mounts the workspace at the data directory. Files root writes there belong to root, so a cleanup step may need sudo.
A data volume keeps the workspace out of the cluster.
And treat a cluster config like a script: don't create clusters from configs that untrusted pull requests can change.
Last, node failure tests. Freeze, cut or shut down a worker, and the test waits until slurmctld marks it down.
With the default timeout, that takes about five minutes, so lower the slurmd timeout to thirty seconds.
So: the action or a verified binary, one realm per job, and a short slurmd timeout for failure tests.
Next up, the controller failover guide. See you there!
